lessons.title: What Is a Container, and Why?

slots.practicalActivity: Install Docker Desktop if it isn't already installed, run docker run hello-world, and open Docker Desktop's Images and Containers tabs to see it listed. Then run the same hello-world image 3 separate times with docker run --name, giving each run a different name, and confirm with docker ps -a that 1 image produced 3 independent containers.
slots.deliverable: A screenshot of Docker Desktop's Images and Containers tabs plus docker ps -a output showing 1 image and 3 separately named containers started from it.

slots.practicalActivity: Write the exact 7-instruction Dockerfile pattern from the lesson (FROM python:3.12-slim, WORKDIR /app, COPY requirements.txt ., RUN pip install -r requirements.txt, COPY . ., EXPOSE 8000, CMD) for a trivial server.py that just prints a message on startup, and confirm docker build completes with no errors.
slots.deliverable: A real Dockerfile following the 7-instruction pattern, with a successful docker build log.

slots.practicalActivity: Build your Dockerfile with docker build -t my-ai-app:1.0 ., then run it with docker run -d --name ai-app -p 8000:8000 -e LOG_LEVEL=debug my-ai-app:1.0. Confirm it with docker ps, stream its logs with docker logs -f ai-app, open a shell inside it with docker exec -it ai-app sh, and stop it with docker stop ai-app.
slots.deliverable: Real terminal output from docker ps, docker logs, docker exec, and docker stop run in sequence against your own container.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a compose.yaml with 2 real services: your app service (build: .) with depends_on set on a redis:7-alpine service. Run docker compose up -d, confirm both with docker compose ps, stream only the api service's logs with docker compose logs -f api, then tear everything down with docker compose down.
slots.deliverable: A working 2-service compose.yaml plus terminal output from up, ps, a single-service logs command, and down.

slots.practicalActivity: Create a real repository on Docker Hub (or GHCR). Run docker login, docker tag my-ai-app:1.0 <yourname>/my-ai-app:1.0, and docker push <yourname>/my-ai-app:1.0 for real, then confirm the pushed image shows up on the registry's own browse page.
slots.deliverable: A real image pushed to a Docker Hub or GHCR repository, confirmed visible in the registry's web UI.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter-ending lab for Docker Fundamentals: starting from a clean folder, write a Dockerfile, build and tag it with a real version (not latest), run it using -p, -e, and -v together in one command, confirm it with docker ps and docker logs, then push the finished image to your registry under that version tag.
slots.deliverable: One project folder taken end to end: a Dockerfile, a version-tagged build, a run combining -p/-e/-v, and a final push to your registry.

slots.practicalActivity: Build the FastAPI inference service from the lesson: app/main.py loading a model.pkl with joblib and exposing POST /predict. Containerize it with the lesson's Dockerfile, add a real .dockerignore excluding .venv/, __pycache__/, and notebooks/, then docker build, docker run -p 8000:8000, and curl -X POST localhost:8000/predict with real feature values to confirm a real prediction comes back.
slots.deliverable: A working containerized FastAPI inference service answering a real curl POST to /predict with an actual prediction value.

slots.practicalActivity: Pin every package in your requirements.txt with == instead of a loose range. Build your Chapter 2 image twice: once baking the model file in with COPY, and once mounting it instead with docker run -v. Compare both images' sizes with docker images and write one sentence on which option you'd pick if the model updated weekly.
slots.deliverable: Two real builds of the same image (baked-in vs. volume-mounted model), their compared sizes, and a one-sentence choice with reasoning.

slots.practicalActivity: Add a fake API key to your app two ways: once via a Dockerfile ENV (the wrong way), and once via docker run -e. Run docker history on the ENV version and confirm the secret is visible in the image's layer history. Fix it by moving the value into a .env file (added to .gitignore) and running with --env-file instead.
slots.deliverable: docker history output proving an ENV-baked secret is recoverable from the image, plus a corrected --env-file run that keeps it out of the image entirely.

slots.practicalActivity: Rewrite your Chapter 2 Dockerfile as a real two-stage build: a builder stage with build-essential installing your pinned requirements.txt via --prefix=/install, and a slim runtime stage that only runs COPY --from=builder /install /usr/local. Compare the final image's size against your single-stage version with docker images.
slots.deliverable: A working multi-stage Dockerfile plus a measured, real before/after image-size comparison against the single-stage version.

slots.practicalActivity: If you have access to an NVIDIA GPU (locally or a cloud VM), build an image FROM nvidia/cuda:12.4.1-runtime-ubuntu22.04 and run docker run --gpus all nvidia/cuda:12.4.1-runtime-ubuntu22.04 nvidia-smi to confirm the GPU is visible inside the container. If no GPU is available, write out the exact commands you'd run and what a successful nvidia-smi output would show, plus one sentence on why omitting --gpus doesn't error, it just silently falls back to CPU.
slots.deliverable: Either real nvidia-smi output captured from inside a container, or a written walkthrough of the exact verification commands and expected output.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter-ending lab for Containerizing AI Applications: combine everything from this chapter into one final image of your Chapter 2 inference service — pinned dependencies, model weights mounted as a volume (not baked in), secrets passed via --env-file, and a multi-stage build — then build, run, and curl it end to end to confirm it still works with all four improvements applied together.
slots.deliverable: One final containerized inference service combining pinned deps, volume-mounted weights, env-file secrets, and a multi-stage build, demonstrated working with a real curl request.

lessons.title: Deploying to a Cloud Container Service

slots.practicalActivity: Push your Chapter 2 image to a registry, then deploy it for real to a managed cloud container service (AWS App Runner, Google Cloud Run, or Azure Container Apps), configuring its build/start command, listening port, CPU/memory, and a health check, until it gives you a real public HTTPS URL.
slots.deliverable: A real, live public HTTPS URL for your deployed container, with a successful request/response against it.

slots.practicalActivity: In front of your deployed service, set up a real API gateway (e.g. AWS API Gateway) with one resource/route forwarding to your backend, deploy it to a stage (e.g. Prod), and get its real invoke URL. Configure a rate and burst limit on that stage, then test the method directly in the gateway console.
slots.deliverable: A working API gateway stage with its own real invoke URL (distinct from your backend's URL) and a configured rate limit, tested successfully in the console.

slots.practicalActivity: Deploy a second ('green') version of your container with one visible change (a different response field or log line), fully running at 0% traffic, then switch 100% of traffic to it at the gateway/load-balancer layer and confirm the cutover. Write 2-3 sentences describing what a real model-equivalence check would need to verify for an AI app that a plain HTTP 200 wouldn't catch.
slots.deliverable: A demonstrated real blue-green cutover between two deployed versions, plus a written note on AI-specific model-equivalence verification.

slots.practicalActivity: If your platform supports it, configure a rolling update with an explicit max surge and max unavailable (e.g. max unavailable 0, max surge 1) and roll out a small code change, watching instances replace a few at a time. Then simulate a bad release and roll it back, and write one paragraph on the AI-specific case where rolling back the application code alone would NOT fix a bad release caused by a newly-promoted model checkpoint instead.
slots.deliverable: A configured rolling update with stated max surge/max unavailable values, a demonstrated rollback, and the written model-vs-code rollback explanation.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter-ending practice for Deployment Patterns: write a one-page deployment-pattern decision memo for your own containerized app — pick blue-green vs. rolling updates, justify it against this chapter's real cost/downtime trade-off, and state exactly what has to be true beforehand (previous image tag kept in the registry, schema compatibility) for your chosen pattern's rollback to actually work.
slots.deliverable: A completed one-page deployment-pattern decision memo naming a stated rollback precondition.

slots.practicalActivity: On your deployed cloud container service, configure a real autoscaling policy with an explicit min and max instance count, choosing a scaling signal (concurrency or CPU) appropriate to your app, and write one sentence justifying each number against the lesson's min-floor/max-ceiling protections.
slots.deliverable: A configured autoscaling policy with explicit min/max instances and a written justification for each number.

slots.practicalActivity: Scale your deployed service down to its minimum (or 0, if allowed) and time, with a stopwatch, how long a fresh request takes once it triggers a cold start. Raise the min-instances floor by 1 and re-time a fresh request to compare. Write one sentence on which mitigation (min floor, pre-warming, or a smaller model) you'd pick for your app's actual latency tolerance.
slots.deliverable: Two real measured cold-start timings (lower min vs. higher min) and a written mitigation choice with reasoning.

slots.practicalActivity: Add a simple exact-match response cache to your containerized app (an in-memory dict keyed on the exact request payload is enough) and call it with the identical request twice, confirming the second call skips your model/logic entirely. Write 2-3 sentences, with a real example pair of differently-worded but same-meaning requests, describing what a semantic cache would additionally catch that your exact-match cache just missed.
slots.deliverable: A working exact-match cache demonstrated with a real repeated request, plus a written semantic-caching example it wouldn't have caught.

slots.practicalActivity: Convert one endpoint of your app to the async job pattern: return a job ID immediately, do the real work in a background task/worker, and let the client poll a /status/<job_id> endpoint for the result. Separately, configure (or document the exact steps to configure) a spend-based budget alert on the cloud account hosting your deployment, independent of your traffic/latency alerts.
slots.deliverable: A working job-ID-plus-polling endpoint pair, plus a configured or documented cost/budget alert distinct from your traffic alerts.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter-ending lab for Scaling & Reliability: on your deployed service, combine this chapter's pieces for real — a justified min/max autoscaling policy, a real health check endpoint the platform actually calls, and either your exact-match cache or your async job pattern wired in — then run a simple real load test (a loop of repeated curl calls) and confirm autoscaling and the health check both behave as configured.
slots.deliverable: A deployed service with autoscaling, a real platform-polled health check, and one additional reliability feature, demonstrated under a simple real load test.

slots.practicalActivity: Scaffold the real FeedbackScope project: a FastAPI app with a POST /analyze endpoint that will load a real Hugging Face transformers sentiment-analysis pipeline and return a label and score. Write out the 5 success criteria from the lesson (clean build, real version tag, public URL, wired health check, justified min/max) as a checklist you'll check off by the wrap-up lesson.
slots.deliverable: The scaffolded FeedbackScope project folder (an app.py stub and requirements.txt) and a written 5-item success-criteria checklist.

lessons.title: Capstone: Containerizing & Deploying a Real AI App

slots.practicalActivity: Build FeedbackScope for real using the lesson's exact multi-stage Dockerfile: a builder stage installing pinned requirements, and a runtime stage that copies the installed packages and runs the model-download line at build time so weights are cached in the image. Tag it with a real version (not latest), push it to a registry, and deploy it to a cloud container service with a GET /health endpoint wired into the platform's health check, until POST /analyze on real feedback text returns a real label and score.
slots.deliverable: FeedbackScope live at a real public URL, returning a real sentiment label and score from a POST /analyze call with actual feedback text.

slots.practicalActivity: Add a concurrency-based autoscaling policy to FeedbackScope with min_instances=1, max_instances=5, and a target concurrency (e.g. 10 requests/instance) you justify from a quick local load test noting where p95 latency started climbing. Make /health actually run a tiny test sentence through the real model instead of just confirming the process is alive, and write one sentence on why you're deliberately skipping semantic caching for this app's traffic pattern.
slots.deliverable: FeedbackScope's live autoscaling policy with justified min/max/target numbers, a health check that exercises the real model, and the written caching decision.

slots.practicalActivity: Write FeedbackScope's README covering what it does with a real example request/response, why the Dockerfile is built the way it is, the autoscaling policy with its justification, and one paragraph on what you'd add next with more time or budget. Rehearse explaining the project out loud, from memory, with a reason for every choice.
slots.deliverable: A complete FeedbackScope README (real example request/response, Dockerfile reasoning, autoscaling justification, next-steps paragraph) and a rehearsed, notes-free verbal walkthrough.

slots.practicalActivity: Final review for Docker & Deployment for AI Applications: push the finished FeedbackScope project (Dockerfile, app code, README) to a real public or private GitHub repository. Without notes, explain out loud the difference between an image and a container, why multi-stage builds matter, the real difference between blue-green and rolling-update rollbacks, and FeedbackScope's own autoscaling numbers and why each one is set the way it is.
slots.deliverable: A public or private GitHub repository containing the finished FeedbackScope project, plus a completed, notes-free self-review covering all five chapters.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After this course, a student can containerize a real AI application end to end — writing a production-grade Dockerfile, managing secrets and model weights correctly, deploying it to a managed cloud container service, and configuring real autoscaling, caching, and rollback strategies — and has shipped FeedbackScope, a live, autoscaled sentiment-analysis API, to a public GitHub repository.
